rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention pattern will identify critical pairs and guide narrower-window and slope comparisons.

Change only gradient duration to measure how the tightly clustered early peaks respond to a shallower slope. This comparison will distinguish slope-sensitive separations from pairs that may require temperature adjustment.

Test temperature selectivity against injection 1 while retaining its fast gradient. The early cluster remains only partly separated by a shallower slope, so a temperature shift may resolve it without a time penalty.

At 60 C only one pair remains below target, with ample time available before the 10-minute threshold. A shallower gradient tests whether that pair can reach R ≥ 1.5 while keeping the last peak within 10 minutes.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so simply lengthening the run is unlikely to help. Raise the starting organic fraction to test a different selectivity window at the best temperature, while monitoring early-peak retention.
Injection 5 achieved the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method, retaining injection 5 as the benchmark if either critical pair falls below R = 1.5.

The 8-minute gradient narrowly missed resolution targets. Lowering its endpoint to 0.85 makes the slope intermediate between injections 5 and 6, potentially restoring full resolution with a shorter elution time than injection 5.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 7’s slope to test whether elution can be accelerated without losing full resolution. The main risks are compression of the early peaks and altered selectivity within the critical cluster; injection 7 remains the faster fully resolved benchmark.

The maximum CRF is already secured, so test the opposite temperature limit for an alternative selectivity pattern that might permit faster gradients. Keeping injection 7’s gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect.

Return to 60 C and test a slope just steeper than the fastest fully resolved method, targeting the resolution boundary. The 0.70 endpoint remains above the last peak’s estimated elution composition, so all peaks should elute during the gradient.

Test whether a modest temperature reduction restores the compressed early pair in injection 8 while retaining its faster, higher-organic window. Injection 10 still has a pair below 1.5 despite its rounded CRF, so injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

At the higher starting organic fraction, only one pair failed at 60 C, and cooling did not help. Test a shallower slope to recover that pair and determine whether this window offers a fully resolved alternative with greater resolution margin.

Return to the better starting fraction and reduce the endpoint one step from injection 10 to restore its marginal pair. This trimmed gradient should retain all peaks within the gradient while providing a fully resolved six-minute program.

The fastest fully resolved method has little resolution margin, and further steepening has caused failure. Test a modestly shallower slope at the successful starting composition to improve the weakest pair while preserving the maximum CRF and a last peak comfortably before 10 minutes.

Injection 12 nearly resolved the higher-starting-organic window; this slightly shallower slope should push its limiting pair above 1.5. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, allowing a direct test of another maximum-CRF method without a time penalty.

Test the remaining intermediate starting composition near the successful window to map the trade-off between the two critical early separations. This slightly steeper gradient explores whether improved early retention can support a faster fully resolved method; injection 7 remains the benchmark.

Refine between injections 7 and 14 with a single endpoint step, seeking more resolution margin than injection 7 without the full time increase of injection 14. The maximum CRF is already achieved, so this tests a practical speed–resolution compromise.

Test a one-step temperature reduction at the fastest confirmed fully resolved gradient to measure its temperature sensitivity directly. This will establish whether maximum CRF requires 60 C or can be retained at a lower operating temperature.

Preserve injection 7’s successful slope through the critical early cluster, but end the gradient after four minutes. This tests whether a shorter program followed by a hold can retain maximum CRF; the late peaks may elute later, so injection 7 remains the speed benchmark.

The shortened program delayed the last peak, leaving injection 7 as the fastest fully resolved method. With maximum CRF secured, test a shallower gradient at the successful starting composition for greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test the single endpoint step above the fastest confirmed fully resolved method to bracket its speed limit directly. This may slightly sacrifice the weakest pair, but will establish whether injection 7 can be accelerated on the available grid.

Trim injection 14’s gradient duration and endpoint while preserving its successful slope and early-pair resolution margin. The last peak should elute near the gradient-to-hold transition, testing a shorter programmed gradient with little change in total elution time.

Test an intermediate slope between injections 14 and 20 to seek additional resolution margin with less delay than injection 20. This should preserve maximum CRF; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
